studies.title: Teenagers' hearts slow down when they scroll before bed — so screens may not be keeping them awake the way we think
studies.ns_score_reason: objective wearable-camera plus heart-rate data directly contradict the "screens cause physiological arousal" story, though the sample is small.
studies.the_study: Researchers in New Zealand filmed the evenings of 70 young people aged 11–14.9 (37% Māori, 42% female) using wearable cameras across four nights, while Fitbit Inspire 2 devices logged heart rate. Median heart rate was substantially *lower* during screen use than during non-screen activity (83 vs. 93 bpm), and social media use closest to bedtime was associated with a further small drop (−3 bpm), while messaging and calls nudged heart rate up (+3 bpm). Pre-bed heart rate was unrelated to sleep outcomes except sleep latency, which rose by about 9 minutes per 10 bpm.
studies.why_it_matters: The dominant public explanation for screens harming teen sleep — that devices leave kids physiologically wound up — gets little support here; the more plausible culprit is simple displacement of bedtime.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a 13-year-old lying in bed on TikTok with a camera on her chest and a heart-rate monitor on her wrist — and a pulse that is calmer than when she was doing homework. The hook: scrolling may be a relaxation ritual, and the sleep problem is about clocks, not cortisol. Call Kim Meredith-Jones and Rachael Taylor at the University of Otago, who have run several objective screen-use studies.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-and-evidence feature for a parenting or education outlet on how wearable cameras are quietly dismantling a decade of self-reported screen-time research — and why the policy debate has run far ahead of the measurements.
studies.caveats: Small N (70), single center, observational within-person design, short monitoring window (four nights), Fitbit-derived heart rate is a proxy for arousal, and findings may not generalize beyond this age band or region.

studies.title: Unusual mental experiences come first, phone dependence follows — via daytime sleepiness
studies.ns_score_reason: a large three-wave cohort reverses the assumed arrow of causation, but everything is self-reported.
studies.the_study: A total of 6,153 Chinese college students (79.7% female; mean age 20.1) reported problematic smartphone use, psychotic-like experiences and excessive daytime sleepiness three times over 12 months. Conventional cross-lagged models showed the usual tangle of associations — but once stable between-person differences were removed, the within-person evidence for a two-way street vanished. What remained was a single pathway: more psychotic-like experiences at wave 1 predicted more daytime sleepiness at wave 2, which predicted heavier problematic smartphone use at wave 3.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that in some young people, heavy phone use is downstream of distress and disrupted sleep rather than its cause — a direct challenge to the simplest version of the "phones are driving youth mental illness" narrative.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reversal: the phone may be the symptom, not the disease. Frame around one student whose odd perceptual experiences and unrelenting daytime fog left the phone as the only thing that fit. The mediation via sleepiness is the mechanistic hook. Call Dongfang Wang at South China Normal University. Be explicit that this is observational and cannot license clinical advice.
studies.wider_angle: A statistics story for a general-interest or data-journalism outlet on how the switch from CLPM to RI-CLPM has been erasing "bidirectional" screen findings across the field — a quiet methodological correction with big public consequences.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation), entirely self-reported measures, heavily female sample of Chinese university students that may not generalize, six-month intervals may miss faster dynamics.

studies.title: Feeling short of time hollows out life's meaning — and the fix is what you aim for, not what you do
studies.ns_score_reason: five studies including two huge naturalistic datasets, an experiment and a successful brief intervention; unusually complete evidence chain.
studies.the_study: Across five studies, researchers linked the chronic feeling of "time poverty" to lower meaning in life: archival data (N=54,568), natural-language analysis of 126,424 social media posts, a validated survey (N=383), an experiment manipulating time-poor context (N=160), and a brief reflection task (N=396). The mechanism was a shrinking of *intrinsic* goal aspirations — growth, relationships, community. Extrinsic goals were also associated with time poverty but had no relationship with meaning; a short reflection on intrinsic goals blunted the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes busyness as a goal-content problem rather than a scheduling problem, and offers a testable, cheap countermeasure.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the language of hurry in social media posts — what 126,000 people actually write when they feel out of time — then the payoff: time scarcity doesn't just crowd out activities, it quietly rewrites what you want. Call Yan Mu at the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Note the experimental studies are lab-scale and short-term.
studies.wider_angle: A work-and-economics feature for a business or long-read outlet on time poverty as a distributional issue — who gets to hold intrinsic goals, and what four-day-week and caregiving policy would need to do to protect meaning rather than just hours.
studies.caveats: Studies 1–3 are cross-sectional/observational; experimental effects are short-term with no follow-up; social media language analysis is a proxy measure; samples are largely Chinese and may not generalize.

studies.title: What you see in your feed pushes your body image around — but your body image barely steers what you look at
studies.ns_score_reason: intensive real-time sampling in a large sample kills the popular "you only see it because you seek it out" defense; still self-reported exposure.
studies.the_study: 858 undergraduates (78.3% women) reported six times a day for a week on their momentary exposure to thinspiration, fitspiration and fatspiration content, plus body dissatisfaction, objectification, appreciation, and urges to restrict or exercise. Viewing thinspiration predicted greater body dissatisfaction; fitspiration predicted *lower* body appreciation; fatspiration predicted stronger urges to exercise. In the reverse direction, only one path was significant — higher body objectification predicted *less* subsequent thinspiration viewing. Gender did not moderate any of it.
studies.why_it_matters: The selectivity argument — that vulnerable people simply seek out this content — gets almost no support in real time, and "fitspiration" looks no safer than thinspiration. The null gender moderation also undercuts the framing of this as a girls' issue.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is asymmetry: content moves the person far more than the person moves the content. Open on a student pinged at 3pm mid-scroll. Ask why fitspiration erodes body *appreciation* even while looking wholesome. Call Isabel Krug at the University of Melbourne.
studies.wider_angle: A platform-accountability piece for a technology or policy outlet: if exposure effects are largely one-directional and gender-neutral, what does that imply for age-gated content rules and recommender audits currently written around teenage girls?
studies.caveats: Undergraduate sample may not generalize; exposure and outcomes both self-reported at the same prompts; associations are momentary and observational; effect sizes not reported in the abstract; one-week window.

studies.title: Watching yourself through the camera's eye may make you less able to feel hunger
studies.ns_score_reason: a plausible, specific mechanistic pathway with longitudinal support, but only two time points and one gender.
studies.the_study: 762 women-identifying college students (353 at follow-up) completed measures of appearance-related social media consciousness (ASMC — the habit of monitoring how you'd look to an online audience), interoceptive sensibility, and eating pathology one month apart. ASMC predicted rising body dissatisfaction but not binge eating or restraint. Crucially, ASMC predicted *reduced acceptance of bodily sensations*, and that reduced acceptance in turn predicted more restrictive eating, with a significant indirect path.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete route from social media habits to restriction that isn't about comparison or thin-ideal internalization — it's about tuning out the body's own signals.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is a strange trade-off: the more attention you pay to how your body *looks* to an imagined feed, the less you accept how it *feels*. Open on the moment of checking a photo before posting. Call April Smith at Auburn University. Frame as mechanism, not clinical advice.
studies.wider_angle: A broader mind-body feature for a health or psychology outlet on interoception as an emerging common currency across anxiety, eating disorders and chronic pain — and whether interoceptive training does anything useful.
studies.caveats: Observational half-longitudinal design (cannot establish causation), women-only college sample that may not generalize, one-month follow-up, self-reported outcomes, substantial attrition between waves.

studies.title: People recovering from anorexia describe a phase of relentless hunger that clinical textbooks don't mention
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely undocumented clinical phenomenon surfaced from patient forums; qualitative and non-representative.
studies.the_study: Researchers pulled 987 posts from r/AnorexiaRecovery (July 2023–January 2024) and thematically analyzed the 92 (9.3%) that described "extreme hunger" during refeeding — a phenomenon absent from the clinical literature. Three themes emerged: anxiety that the hunger was abnormal and signaled binge eating disorder; extreme hunger as a threat to recovery, prompting distress, suicidal thoughts, renewed restriction and relapse; and a perceived vacuum of professional guidance, driving people to online sources instead.
studies.why_it_matters: A predictable, biologically plausible stage of recovery is going unexplained by clinicians, and the resulting fear appears to push people back into restriction — a fixable gap.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the vacuum: thousands of people are asking a subreddit a question their clinicians have never named. Open on a single anonymized post. The story writes itself as patient-generated knowledge outpacing the literature. Call Léa Langanay or Antoine Lamer in Lille. Do not present forum accounts as prevalence data.
studies.wider_angle: A media/health-information feature for a specialist outlet on Reddit as an unlicensed clinical evidence source — how researchers are now mining forums for symptoms medicine has failed to record, and the ethics of doing so without consent.
studies.caveats: Qualitative analysis of public posts, no demographic or diagnostic verification, self-selected online population that may not generalize, no prevalence estimate, no control group.

studies.title: Ozempic has been absorbed into pro-eating-disorder Twitter as everyday, normalized talk
studies.ns_score_reason: highly topical and the first systematic look at GLP-1 discourse in this community, but a small, descriptive corpus.
studies.the_study: Using netnography, researchers retrieved public posts on X containing both "Ozempic" and "edtwt" (the eating-disorder Twitter tag) from August 2024 to July 2025, analyzing 255 after exclusions. The single largest theme was normalization and cultural saturation (28.6%) — Ozempic treated as unremarkable background. Personal narratives covered curiosity (19.2%), intent to use (11.8%), active use or experimentation (11.4%) and access (9.0%). Risk warnings and information sharing made up just 3.5%.
studies.why_it_matters: GLP-1 drugs are entering the most vulnerable online communities almost entirely without countervailing risk information, and access appears to be a live, discussed problem rather than a hypothetical one.
studies.pitch_angle: The number to lead on is 3.5% — the share of posts containing any risk warning, against 28.6% treating the drug as normal. Frame as: a prescription medication has been culturally absorbed by a community organized around restriction. Call Jennifer Couturier at McMaster. Avoid amplifying access routes.
studies.wider_angle: A pharmaceutical-regulation investigation for a health-policy or business outlet: how telehealth prescribing, compounded semaglutide and grey-market supply intersect with online communities that platforms have repeatedly failed to moderate.
studies.caveats: Small corpus (255 posts), single platform, descriptive content analysis with no user characteristics, no way to verify who posted or whether stated intentions became behavior, time-limited sampling window.

studies.title: Classmates can reliably name the school's "influencers" — and those teens are both kinder and more aggressive than their peers
studies.ns_score_reason: a new peer-nomination method that sidesteps self-reported screen time, though single-school and cross-sectional.
studies.the_study: 331 seventh and eighth graders in a small Midwestern US community nominated which classmates were most visible on social media. These peer nominations corresponded moderately with the nominees' own reports of social media use — and predicted higher levels of prosocial behavior, higher physical, verbal and relational aggression, and more self-reported substance use.
studies.why_it_matters: It validates a way of measuring adolescent social media prominence that doesn't depend on teens estimating their own screen time, and it complicates the picture of the visible teen: social capital and social harm travel together.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is that the most-followed kid in year 8 is simultaneously the most helpful and the most aggressive — visibility looks like a form of social power, with everything that implies. Open on the nomination exercise itself. Call Lara Mayeux at the University of Oklahoma.
studies.wider_angle: A schools feature for an education outlet on peer-nomination methods generally — what happens when researchers ask children to map their own social hierarchies, and what teachers could learn from those maps.
studies.caveats: Single school in one small community (population may not generalize), cross-sectional and observational, substance use and social media use self-reported, no measure of what the visible teens actually posted.

studies.title: A substantial minority of people press "like" specifically to hurt someone
studies.ns_score_reason: a delightfully counterintuitive four-study package on an unstudied behavior; evidence is mostly survey-based.
studies.the_study: Four studies examined "counter-valenced liking" — using the like button on bad news about a rival. Study 1 used five years of archival data on likes attached to sports teams' negative posts, showing the behavior increasing over time. Study 2 (qualitative) found a substantial minority admitting to it, most citing schadenfreude. Study 3 confirmed a correlation between trait schadenfreude and liking negative outcomes, including injuries. Study 4 found that people most bothered by receiving such likes are more likely to do it themselves, and a notable number said they did it explicitly to hurt the other party.
studies.why_it_matters: A button designed to signal approval has been repurposed as a low-cost weapon — a neat case study in how platform affordances get inverted by users, and how content-moderation systems that read likes as positive signals are misreading them.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the moment a fan sees a rival's star player carried off the pitch — and taps the heart. The hook: "engagement" metrics can't tell joy from cruelty. Call Devin Lunt at Morehead State University.
studies.wider_angle: A technology feature for a general-interest outlet on the semantics of reaction buttons — why platforms keep adding emoji and keep failing to capture what users mean, and what that does to recommendation algorithms trained on those signals.
studies.caveats: Largely self-report and cross-sectional, sports-fandom context may not generalize to political or personal contexts, no behavioral measure of actual liking in Studies 2–4, sample sizes and demographics not specified in the abstract.

studies.title: Adding a social network to an eating-disorder app didn't help teens — and unguided self-help worked about as well as coaching
studies.ns_score_reason: a randomized three-arm test of a widely assumed "peer support helps" premise, though a pilot without a no-treatment arm.
studies.the_study: 148 teens with or at high risk for eating disorders, recruited via social media and an online screen, were randomized to app-based self-help, guided self-help with a coach, or guided self-help plus a peer social networking component, with follow-up to 6 months. There were no significant between-group differences on global eating disorder psychopathology; all groups improved substantially (d = −0.93 from baseline to 6 months). Binge eating fell in all arms, but fastest in the guided self-help arm — the one *without* the social network.
studies.why_it_matters: Peer-networking features are routinely bolted onto youth mental health apps on the assumption they boost engagement and outcomes; this pilot finds no benefit, and hints the simpler product may be better for binge eating.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the null that matters commercially: the social feature didn't add anything. Open on a teen using a stripped-down app alone at midnight. Call Patricia Cavazos-Rehg or Ellen Fitzsimmons-Craft at Washington University in St. Louis, and press on why peer contact might be neutral or counterproductive in this population.
studies.wider_angle: A digital-health business piece for a specialist or trade outlet on the "engagement feature" arms race in youth mental health apps, and how rarely those features are tested against a plain-vanilla control.
studies.caveats: Pilot RCT, small N (148) for a three-arm design, no inactive control so improvement over time cannot be attributed to the apps, several authors declare consultancy relationships with digital health companies (Woebot, Kooth, Google Health, Rissana, PredictView), recruitment via social media may skew the sample.

studies.title: Four in five adolescents who self-harm or restrict say they sometimes do it to feel *worse*
studies.ns_score_reason: directly challenges a foundational assumption in the emotion-regulation model of self-harm, but the sample is small and online-recruited.
studies.the_study: 137 adolescents (mean age 15.1, 75% female), recruited online via social media into a longitudinal study, reported on the functions of restrictive eating, binge eating, purging and non-suicidal self-injury. The field has assumed these behaviors are pro-hedonic — done to reduce negative feeling. Instead, 81% endorsed at least one *contra*-hedonic function: doing it to increase or sustain negative affect, or to dampen positive affect. Contra-hedonic motives were strongest for non-suicidal self-injury and consistently tied to a desire to self-punish.
studies.why_it_matters: If a large share of self-destructive behavior is aimed at feeling worse rather than better, treatments built entirely around teaching alternative distress-reduction skills are targeting the wrong function for many teens.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the inversion of a textbook assumption: the goal isn't relief, it's punishment. Open on the survey item that adolescents kept endorsing. Call Shirley Wang at Yale. Frame carefully — this is a description of motives, not a treatment claim, and needs Samaritans-style signposting.
studies.wider_angle: A clinical-practice feature for a psychology or medical outlet on functional analysis in adolescent mental health — how therapies get built on an assumed function, and what happens to dialectical behavior therapy's skills modules if self-punishment is the real driver.
studies.caveats: Small N (137), predominantly White and female sample recruited via social media (may not generalize), cross-sectional self-report of motives within a larger study, secondary analysis, no clinical verification of behaviors.

studies.title: Identifying with an online group makes you more likely to start measuring yourself against others
studies.ns_score_reason: five-country longitudinal panel with within-person analysis; a rare piece of evidence on *why* people compare, though self-reported.
studies.the_study: Using longitudinal survey data from adults aged 18–75 in Finland (N=1,541), France (N=1,561), Germany (N=1,529), Ireland (N=1,112) and Poland (N=1,533), researchers tracked whether identifying with online groups and networks predicted a person's orientation toward comparing their abilities with others. It did — both between and within individuals over time — and the relationship was partly mediated by the motive to verify one's own self-concept.
studies.why_it_matters: Social comparison is usually treated as a fixed personality trait or as a passive consequence of exposure to feeds; this suggests it is actively cultivated by belonging to online groups, which reframes the target for any "healthy social media" intervention.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive bit is that belonging — usually cast as the protective factor — is what ramps up comparison. Open on someone joining a running or parenting group online for support and finding themselves ranked. Call Atte Oksanen's group at Tampere University, which runs the panel.
studies.wider_angle: A social-psychology feature for a longer-form outlet revisiting Festinger's 1954 comparison theory at 70 — and how digital group life has made a supposedly egocentric process into a fundamentally social one.
studies.caveats: All self-reported, observational (cannot establish causation), European adult samples only, effect sizes not given in the abstract, mediation inferred from panel data rather than experiment.

studies.title: The strongest predictor of compulsive short-video use isn't the pull of the videos — it's overestimating your own self-control
studies.ns_score_reason: a nice metacognitive twist on the flow literature, weakened by a cross-sectional self-report design.
studies.the_study: Survey data from 842 short-form video users were analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling, treating "flow" not as the classic optimal experience but as a passive state with maladaptive components (affective reliance, loss of self-reflection, telepresence). Overestimation of one's own self-control emerged as the strongest driver of compulsive use — exceeding the total effect of flow itself — and flow raised compulsive use partly by inflating that overconfidence.
studies.why_it_matters: It relocates the problem from the content to a metacognitive illusion: the belief that you could stop whenever you wanted is itself what keeps you scrolling.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on "I can stop any time" as the mechanism, not the excuse. Open with a reader mentally estimating how long they've been on TikTok, then the gap between estimate and reality. The reframing of flow — psychology's poster child for the good life — as something that can be hollow and passive is the second hook. Call Chei Sian Lee at Nanyang Technological University.
studies.wider_angle: A design-critique piece for a technology outlet on whether screen-time dashboards and app timers work at all if the core problem is a confidence illusion rather than ignorance of the numbers.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation), all self-reported including the outcome, sample demographics unspecified, latent-variable model heavily dependent on the novel reconceptualization of flow, no behavioral usage data.

studies.title: Short-form video use predicts disordered eating four months later — in working nurses, not teenagers
studies.ns_score_reason: usefully extends media-effects research beyond students to a working adult profession; modest sample with attrition.
studies.the_study: 400 registered female nurses at a hospital in Wuhan, China were surveyed at baseline, with 270 retained at four-month follow-up. Baseline short-form video use predicted disordered eating at follow-up indirectly, through increased body dissatisfaction. The pathway was stronger among nurses reporting high perceived media pressure and thin-ideal internalization.
studies.why_it_matters: Almost all evidence on social media and eating pathology comes from adolescents and students; this shows the same mechanism operating in shift-working health professionals in their working lives.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is who, not what: the people we assume are inoculated by health literacy aren't. Open on a nurse decompressing with short videos after a night shift. Call Wu Hong or Qingqi Li at Central China Normal University. Note this is prospective but observational.
studies.wider_angle: An occupational-health feature for a nursing or workplace outlet on appearance pressure inside healthcare — a workforce that is majority female, heavily shift-based, and rarely studied as a body-image risk group.
studies.caveats: Single hospital, female-only, two waves with 32.5% attrition, self-reported exposure and outcomes, observational design (cannot establish causation), findings may not generalize outside China.

studies.title: One capacity — the ability to get started — sits underneath anxiety, depression, drinking and compulsive social media use
studies.ns_score_reason: a large, well-analyzed transdiagnostic study, but cross-sectional self-report and a technical framing that needs work to sell.
studies.the_study: 1,997 community adults completed measures of emotion regulation, dispositional self-regulation, psychological flexibility, mentalization, attachment and childhood maltreatment, alongside symptoms of anxiety, depression, alcohol use disorder and problematic social media use. Bayesian model averaging identified *initiatory* self-control — the ability to start goal-directed behavior, as distinct from inhibiting unwanted behavior — as the only predictor credibly associated with all four outcomes. Emotional abuse and anxious attachment tracked anxiety, depression and problematic social media use; psychological flexibility mattered for the internalizing conditions but not the behavioral ones.
studies.why_it_matters: The dominant framing of problematic social media use as a failure of restraint may be backwards — the shared deficit looks like difficulty initiating, and that is a different intervention target.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the distinction most people have never heard: stopping and starting are separate abilities, and it's the starting that's broken. Open on someone who can't put the phone down and equally can't begin the task waiting behind it. Call Tania Moretta at eCampus University.
studies.wider_angle: A conceptual feature for a psychiatry or science-policy outlet on the RDoC project a decade on — whether process-based, dimension-first psychiatry is actually replacing diagnostic categories, and what studies like this one do and don't demonstrate.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation), all self-reported including retrospective childhood maltreatment, community sample recruited without stated sampling frame, no clinical diagnoses.

studies.title: A four-stage map of how recommender systems and AI companions can escort someone toward violence
studies.ns_score_reason: timely and rigorous synthesis with concrete governance proposals, but it is a theoretical review with no new data.
studies.the_study: A synthesis in a leading review journal integrates radicalization process models with research on personality and social risk factors, recommender systems and generative AI into a four-stage framework: Exposure (virality and recommendation create initial attraction to extreme content), Reinforcement (filter bubbles and AI bot swarms manufacture a synthetic consensus), Group Integration (ideologically homogeneous clusters plus AI companions supply belonging and readiness to act), and Violent Extremist Action. The authors specify which known vulnerability factors bite at which stage and propose stage-matched policy measures.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives regulators and researchers a stage-specific vocabulary, and flags AI companions and bot swarms — not just recommendation — as an underrated part of the pipeline.
studies.pitch_angle: The novel element is "synthetic consensus": bot swarms making a fringe view feel like the majority to one user. Open there rather than on the familiar rabbit-hole imagery. Call Jonas Kunst at BI Norwegian Business School. Be clear this is a framework awaiting empirical test, not evidence that AI is radicalizing people at scale.
studies.wider_angle: A regulatory feature for a policy or technology outlet on whether the EU Digital Services Act and AI Act contain anything that touches the Reinforcement and Group Integration stages, or whether they only regulate Exposure.
studies.caveats: Theoretical review with no new empirical data; the framework is untested as a whole; causal claims about AI's contribution remain inferential; risk of overstating a still-rare outcome.

studies.title: Real grooming conversations from court files reveal two very different kinds of offender
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely new dataset that replaces two-decade-old decoy transcripts, though the analysis is preliminary.
studies.the_study: Almost all research on online child grooming rests on Perverted Justice Foundation transcripts collected nearly 20 years ago, in which the "minors" were adults posing as children. Polish researchers assembled a new corpus of conversations between suspected offenders and real minors, drawn from criminal cases reviewed by Polish courts, and compared two offender profiles — hypersexual and intimacy-seeking — on communication strategy, concealment technique, requests made, and the responses those requests drew from the children.
studies.why_it_matters: The evidence base underpinning detection tools and prevention advice was built on simulated conversations from a pre-smartphone internet; this is the first serious attempt to check whether it holds with real interactions.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the methodological scandal hiding in plain sight — that the field's canonical dataset contains no actual children and predates social media as we know it. Open on what changes when the transcripts are real. Call Zuzanna Cieślińska at NASK in Warsaw. Handle detail with extreme care; do not publish tactics in usable form.
studies.wider_angle: An investigation for a technology or security outlet on the automated grooming-detection classifiers now sold to platforms and schools — how many were trained on the old decoy corpus, and what that means for their false-negative rates.
studies.caveats: Preliminary exploratory analysis, sample size not stated, Polish court cases only (population may not generalize), cases that reach court are unrepresentative of grooming overall, profile categories imposed by the researchers.

studies.title: Indigenous Wayuu people describe globalized beauty ideals arriving with the internet — and cultural pride pushing back
studies.ns_score_reason: a rare natural experiment in real time on a badly underrepresented population; qualitative and small.
studies.the_study: Five focus groups with 29 Wayuu participants in Colombia (aged 18–68; 23 women, 6 men) explored appearance ideals during a period of rapidly expanding internet access, migration and economic change. Reflexive thematic analysis identified intersecting appearance pressures (social media, family expectations, discrimination from non-Indigenous peers), negotiation and resistance ranging from restrictive eating to explicit affirmation of cultural identity, and a shifting role for appearance tied to education and connectivity. Cultural pride and collective belonging appeared to buffer against internalizing external ideals.
studies.why_it_matters: It documents the arrival of globalized appearance ideals as it happens, and identifies a protective factor — collective cultural identity — that individual-level media literacy programs don't touch.
studies.pitch_angle: The through-line is that we are watching a decades-old natural experiment run again, this time via smartphones rather than television. Open on a Wayuu participant describing what changed when the signal arrived. Call Ana María Chamorro Coneo at Universidad del Norte or Lynda Boothroyd at Durham, who has run comparable work in Nicaragua.
studies.wider_angle: A global-development feature for an international or anthropology outlet on connectivity programs in Indigenous territories — what public health considerations, if any, accompany the rollout of mobile internet.
studies.caveats: Qualitative with 29 participants, single community, no quantitative body-image measures, retrospective accounts of change, findings not generalizable to other Indigenous groups.

studies.title: "Toxic positivity" finally gets a definition — four dimensions, and social media as a chief driver
studies.ns_score_reason: turns a viral internet phrase into a specified psychological construct, which is genuinely useful; but it's a scoping review with thin empirical backing.
studies.the_study: A scoping review charted 59 academic and grey-literature sources published from January 2011 to June 2024 to define toxic positivity. The synthesis casts it as a socially enforced, overgeneralized norm compelling the performance of happiness in all situations, with four dimensions: emotional suppression, emotional invalidation, unrealistic optimism, and disingenuous happiness. Named antecedents include social media influence, cultural and societal expectations, misinterpretation of positive psychology, and self-protection.
studies.why_it_matters: Not much changes tomorrow, but it opens a line of enquiry: with a definition and dimensions there is now something to build a validated scale around and test empirically.
studies.pitch_angle: The story is a concept graduating from Instagram caption to research construct, and the awkward finding that positive psychology's own popularization is implicated as a cause. Open on the "good vibes only" post under a bereavement announcement. Call Devika Premlal at Christ University, Bangalore, and press on what the measurement study will look like.
studies.wider_angle: An intellectual-history piece for a general-interest or culture outlet tracing the line from Seligman's positive psychology through corporate wellness to the backlash — who profited, what got distorted, and whether the researchers recognize what became of their field.
studies.caveats: Scoping review, includes grey literature alongside peer-reviewed work, English-language only, no validated measurement instrument exists so all conclusions are conceptual, no effect estimates.

studies.title: Vivid "what if" thoughts after sexual assault track with worse trauma symptoms months later
studies.ns_score_reason: first longitudinal test of counterfactual thinking after trauma, with a hard-to-reach sample; heavy attrition limits it.
studies.the_study: 452 people who had experienced sexual assault in the previous year (437 women, 15 men; mean age 26.2), recruited both from Sexual Assault Care Centres and via social media, were assessed at baseline, three months (N=216) and six months (N=232). Latent growth curve models found that both the frequency and vividness of counterfactual "what if" thinking at baseline were associated with persistently higher posttraumatic stress, though not with the rate of symptom change. Vividness — not frequency — was tied to time-specific spikes in symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that how *real* the imagined alternative feels matters more than how often the mind returns to it, which points therapy toward the sensory quality of these thoughts rather than their frequency.
studies.pitch_angle: The distinction between frequency and vividness is the surprise, and it's counterintuitive — thinking about it more isn't the problem; seeing it clearly is. Recruiting through social media also captured survivors who never sought help, a group usually invisible in this literature. Call Ines Blix at the Norwegian Center for Violence and Traumatic Stress Studies. Handle with appropriate care and signposting.
studies.wider_angle: A cognitive-science feature for a psychology or long-read outlet on mental imagery as a clinical target across PTSD, depression and craving — the growing case that vividness, not content, is what makes intrusive thoughts hurt.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation), roughly 50% attrition by follow-up, self-reported counterfactual thinking measured with non-standardized items, overwhelmingly female Norwegian sample, six-month follow-up only.

studies.title: Rough sex is now common among young people — and most say they first learned about it from porn and social media
studies.ns_score_reason: an authoritative synthesis of a genuinely under-reported public health question, but a review rather than new data.
studies.the_study: Herbenick and Galper review the conceptual and empirical literature on "rough sex," drawing on multi-country prevalence data. They tackle the definitional problem (including what "consensual rough sex" means), document demographic patterns, and review health consequences of specific practices — sexual choking and smothering carry serious risks. Young people consistently report first learning about these practices as adolescents from pornography, social media and mainstream media, and clinicians report seeing more marks and bruises attributed to them.
studies.why_it_matters: A set of behaviors with plausible neurological risk has become normalized in a single generation, faster than sex education, clinical guidance or policy has adapted.
studies.pitch_angle: The angle for Mind is the brain: repeated restriction of blood flow to the brain in young people, and what the evidence does and does not yet show about cumulative effects. Open in a sexuality educator's classroom fielding a question they weren't trained for. Call Debby Herbenick at Indiana University. Avoid moralizing; report the risk evidence as it stands.
studies.wider_angle: An education-policy investigation for a news or current-affairs outlet on the gap between what teenagers learn from feeds and what the curriculum covers — with international comparison of how school programs have or haven't responded.
studies.caveats: Narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis; prevalence data drawn from heterogeneous surveys with differing definitions; the authors themselves flag major limitations in the underlying evidence base; causal role of media exposure is self-reported and retrospective.

studies.title: A new scale tries to measure how trapped people feel by their own technology
studies.ns_score_reason: the "digital coercion" construct is a fresh angle on tech and distress, but this is a small psychometric first pass.
studies.the_study: Researchers at Mount Sinai developed the Digital Coercion Scale to capture perceived loss of autonomy in the face of unavoidable technology, and administered it to 89 psychiatric inpatients alongside depression, anxiety, OCD and suicide-risk measures. Internal consistency was high (α = 0.925) and factor analysis found five factors. Scores correlated with depression, obsessive-compulsive symptoms and the Revised Suicide Crisis Inventory — most strongly with its Entrapment, Affective Disturbance and Social Withdrawal subscales — but were unrelated to suicidal ideation.
studies.why_it_matters: It names something distinct from "addiction": not craving the phone but feeling compelled by a system you cannot opt out of. Whether that construct predicts anything clinically useful is entirely open.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the reframing — the problem isn't that you can't stop, it's that you were never given the option to. The entrapment correlation is the interesting thread, since entrapment is central to current models of suicide risk. Call Igor Galynker at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. Do not imply the scale predicts suicide; it did not correlate with ideation.
studies.wider_angle: A digital-rights piece for a technology or civil-liberties outlet on compulsory digitization — banking, healthcare, school, government services — and the mental health cost of removing the non-digital option, especially for older and disabled people.
studies.caveats: Small N (89), single-center psychiatric inpatients (population may not generalize), cross-sectional, no test-retest or predictive validity, no comparison group, self-reported social media use captured by only two items.

studies.title: A three-session writing exercise delivered through WeChat reduced trauma symptoms — and the sophisticated version was no better than the simple one
studies.ns_score_reason: real-world randomized delivery inside a mainstream messaging platform is genuinely novel, but the absence of an inactive control blunts the finding.
studies.the_study: Between December 2021 and August 2022, 1,526 Chinese adults were screened for posttraumatic stress symptoms through a Tencent mini-program; 211 eligible participants were randomized to Guided Narrative Technique-Writing (n=100) or plain Expressive Writing (n=111) — three self-directed daily writing sessions, entirely unsupported by any human. Attrition was 64.5% overall, but 77% of those who actually started finished. Both arms showed significant within-group symptom reductions (d = −0.43 and −0.58), with no difference between them.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows scalable mental health support can be embedded in a platform a billion people already use — while providing another data point that elaborate protocols often fail to beat simple ones.
studies.pitch_angle: The story is delivery, not content: therapy-adjacent tools arriving where people already are, with no clinician in the loop. Open on the mini-program screening question. Then the honest twist — the fancy guided version added nothing. Call Yinyin Zang at Peking University, and be clear the improvements can't be attributed to the intervention without an inactive control.
studies.wider_angle: A global mental health feature for a health or international outlet on super-app-based care delivery in China, India and Brazil, and the governance questions when a private messaging platform becomes a mental health channel.
studies.caveats: No inactive control condition, so within-group improvement cannot be attributed to the interventions; 64.5% attrition; self-reported primary outcome (PTSD Checklist-Short); one-month maximum follow-up; pandemic-era Chinese sample may not generalize.

studies.title: When you promote free school meals on Facebook, roughly as many parents reject the message as accept it
studies.journal: Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior
studies.ns_score_reason: a small but instructive window into why public health messaging fails on social platforms; modest scope.
studies.the_study: Researchers content-analyzed the reactions and comments of 404 parents of grade 1–5 children to a Facebook campaign encouraging participation in universal school meals programs during the 2024–25 school year. Acceptance appeared in 34% of comments, focused on money saved, convenience and social benefit. Rejection appeared in 29% — mostly asserting that school food is unhealthy or poor quality, with some parents questioning the posts' credibility and demanding references and statistics.
studies.why_it_matters: It quantifies the credibility problem facing public health messaging on social platforms: nearly a third of engaged parents pushed back, and a visible subset wanted citations before they'd believe a government-adjacent claim.
studies.pitch_angle: The psychological hook is source distrust in the comment section — parents demanding evidence from a public health campaign in a way they wouldn't from an influencer. Open on a single comment thread. Call Anna Grummon at Stanford. Frame as message reception, not as evidence about school food quality.
studies.wider_angle: A public-communications piece for a policy or journalism outlet on whether health agencies should be advertising on platforms at all, given that every campaign now comes with a built-in, publicly visible opposition.
studies.caveats: Content analysis of self-selected commenters (not a representative parent sample), single platform and campaign, no behavioral outcome — nobody measured whether meal participation actually changed, US states with universal school meals only.

citation_table.journal: Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior

trends_raw: _No prior digest on this topic to compare against yet — this is the first run._
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Half a dozen studies in this batch are not new findings about social media so much as new *measurements* of it — and the better the measurement, the more the standard causal story bends. Wearable cameras plus heart-rate logging find teenagers are calmer, not aroused, while scrolling before bed ("Teenagers' hearts slow down when they scroll before bed", PMID 41556268); a random-intercept cross-lagged model in 6,153 students erases the usual "bidirectional" tangle and leaves phone use as the downstream consequence of distress and daytime sleepiness (PMID 42636649); six-times-daily sampling of 858 undergraduates shows feed content moves body image while body image barely steers what people look at, killing the self-selection defense (PMID 42537570); and peer nomination replaces teens' own screen-time guesses entirely (PMID 42552601). Meanwhile the mechanism studies relocate the problem away from "can't stop": overconfidence in one's own self-control beats content pull as a predictor of compulsive short-video use (PMID 42608804), initiatory rather than inhibitory self-control is the shared thread across anxiety, depression, drinking and problematic use (PMID 42285011), and a new "digital coercion" scale reframes distress as entrapment in systems you cannot opt out of (PMID 42585824).

**Why pitch this now:** Legislation on age gates, phone bans and recommender audits is being written on top of a decade of self-reported screen-time research, exactly as the objective and within-person methods arrive to tell us which of those effects survive scrutiny — and which reverse.

**Angle:** A methods-and-evidence feature for an intelligent general reader: follow the instruments (chest cameras, Fitbits, experience-sampling pings, peer nominations, RI-CLPM) and show what each one adds or subtracts from the harm case, ending on what actually holds up — content exposure effects on body image, and the metacognitive illusion of control. Written for parents, teachers and policymakers who have absorbed the headline version and not the corrections.

**Potential headlines:**
- What chest cameras and heart monitors show teenagers actually doing with their phones at bedtime
- The screen-time effects that disappear when you stop asking people to estimate their screen time
- The phone advice you've been given rests on measurements researchers are now discarding

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — a natural fit for an instrument-led story that reappraises a field readers have followed closely through the youth-mental-health debate.
- **Undark** — built for exactly this kind of "how do we know what we know" scrutiny of a policy-relevant evidence base, including the RI-CLPM correction.
- **The Atlantic** — has hosted the loudest phones-and-teens argument; a measurement-first piece is a genuinely new intervention in it rather than another round of the same fight.
- **BBC Future** — parenting-adjacent readership, and the bedtime heart-rate and body-image sampling findings give it concrete, testable takeaways.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Social Media — August 2026
**Checked:** 2026-08-25 | **Studies reviewed:** 24
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-08-25

---

### Study 1: Teenagers' hearts slow down when they scroll before bed — so screens may not be keeping them awake the way we think
**PMID:** 41556268 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

All core numbers check out: N=70, ages 11–14.9, 37% Māori, 42% female, four nights, Fitbit Inspire 2, 83 vs 93 BPM, −3 BPM for social media, +3 BPM for communication, sleep latency +9 min per 10 BPM. Journal, issue and epub date are correct.

**Issue A. Invented comparison in the pitch scene** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and a pulse that is calmer than when she was doing homework"
- **Abstract says:** "Median heart rate was lower during screen use than during non-screen activities (83 BPM, [IQR: 77-91] vs. 93 [IQR: 87-100])."
- **Problem:** The contrast measured was screen use vs. all non-screen activity. Homework is never named, and much homework is itself screen-based, so the scene attributes a specific comparison to the study that it did not make.
- **Suggested fix:** "and a pulse that is calmer than during her non-screen evening activities"

**Issue B. NS fit score sits slightly high for the size of the claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — objective wearable-camera plus heart-rate data directly contradict the 'screens cause physiological arousal' story, though the sample is small."
- **Abstract says:** "differences were small and effects on sleep only modest"; N=70 over four nights, heart rate via consumer wearable.
- **Problem:** A "overturns prior research" claim resting on 70 adolescents, four nights, and Fitbit-derived heart rate is a large claim on modest evidence, and the authors themselves describe the differences as small.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10, with the fit line noting that the authors characterise the differences as small and the sleep effects as modest.

---

### Study 2: Unusual mental experiences come first, phone dependence follows — via daytime sleepiness
**PMID:** 42636649 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=6,153, 79.7% female, mean age 20.06, three waves at six-month intervals, CLPM vs RI-CLPM contrast, and the PLEs(T1)→EDS(T2)→PSU(T3) pathway are all reported accurately. Corresponding author and institution are correct.

**Issue A. "Overturns prior research" mislabels the novelty** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "few studies have specifically investigated the bidirectional relationship between problematic smartphone use (PSU) and psychotic-like experiences (PLEs)"
- **Problem:** There was little prior work to overturn. What the study does is apply RI-CLPM and find no within-person support for bidirectionality — a methodological correction to an assumption, not a reversal of an established literature. The digest body ("the usual tangle of associations") implies a settled prior finding the abstract does not describe.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** New method applied to an under-tested question — first RI-CLPM test of the PSU–PLE relationship, which finds no within-person bidirectionality"

*Note: the wider-angle claim that "the switch from CLPM to RI-CLPM has been erasing 'bidirectional' screen findings across the field" is unverifiable from this abstract alone.*

---

### Study 3: Feeling short of time hollows out life's meaning — and the fix is what you aim for, not what you do
**PMID:** 42541341 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

All five sample sizes (54,568; 126,424; 383; 160; 396) match, as does the mediation via intrinsic goal aspirations, the null for extrinsic goals on meaning, and the Study 5 reflection task. Author affiliation correct.

**Issue A. Study 1's outcome was a proxy, not meaning in life** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "researchers linked the chronic feeling of 'time poverty' to lower meaning in life: archival data (N=54,568)"
- **Abstract says:** "Study 1 provided initial archival evidence linking perceived time poverty to a proxy for meaninglessness-related experience (N = 54,568)"
- **Problem:** The largest dataset in the package did not measure meaning in life; it used a proxy for meaninglessness-related experience. Presenting it as a direct link inflates the strength of the headline number.
- **Suggested fix:** "archival data linking time poverty to a proxy for meaninglessness-related experience (N=54,568)"

**Issue B. "The fix" overstates a single brief lab task** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and the fix is what you aim for, not what you do"
- **Abstract says:** "Study 5 showed that enhancing intrinsic goal aspirations through a brief reflection task attenuated this negative effect (N = 396)."
- **Problem:** "Attenuated" in a short lab study with no follow-up is not "the fix." The subhead promises a remedy the data only gesture at.
- **Suggested fix:** "and a brief shift in what you aim for may soften it"

*Note: the caveat "samples are largely Chinese" is unverifiable from the abstract only (author affiliations are Chinese, but participant nationality is not stated).*

---

### Study 4: What you see in your feed pushes your body image around — but your body image barely steers what you look at
**PMID:** 42537570 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=858, 78.3% women, six prompts a day for seven days, and all four directional findings (thinspiration→dissatisfaction; fitspiration→lower appreciation; fatspiration→exercise urges; objectification→less thinspiration viewing) are reported correctly.

**Issue A. "No safer" is a comparison the study did not make** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and 'fitspiration' looks no safer than thinspiration"
- **Abstract says:** "viewing thinspiration content predicted greater body dissatisfaction; viewing fitspiration content predicted lower body appreciation"
- **Problem:** The two content types predicted different outcomes; no head-to-head test of magnitude is reported, and the abstract gives no effect sizes. The pitch angle compounds this with causal wording ("why fitspiration *erodes* body appreciation") for momentary associational data.
- **Suggested fix:** "and fitspiration carries its own signal — lower body appreciation — rather than looking benign"; in the pitch, "why fitspiration tracks with lower body *appreciation*"

**Issue B. Gender moderation null stated more broadly than tested** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Gender did not moderate any of it."
- **Abstract says:** "Gender did not moderate inter-individual variation in these momentary relationships."
- **Problem:** The null applies specifically to between-person variation in momentary associations; the authors explicitly flag that gender differences may still appear in cumulative exposure or trait-level self-evaluations. The "Why it matters" line ("undercuts the framing of this as a girls' issue") leans on the broader reading.
- **Suggested fix:** "Gender did not moderate between-person variation in these momentary relationships — though the authors note it may still matter for cumulative exposure."

---

### Study 5: Watching yourself through the camera's eye may make you less able to feel hunger
**PMID:** 42537569 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N figures (T1 762; T2 353), one-month interval, women-identifying college students, half-longitudinal mediation model and the significant indirect effect are all accurate. Author and institution correct.

**Issue A. Headline names the wrong construct** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Watching yourself through the camera's eye may make you less able to feel hunger"
- **Abstract says:** "ASMC also predicted decreases in interoceptive sensibility, specifically a decreased acceptance of somatic sensations"
- **Problem:** The measured variable was self-reported *acceptance* of bodily sensations, not the ability to detect them, and nothing hunger-specific was measured. "Less able to feel hunger" implies an interoceptive accuracy deficit the study did not test. "Make you" also imports causation into a half-longitudinal observational design.
- **Suggested fix:** "Monitoring how you'd look to an online audience tracks with accepting your body's signals less — and eating less"

**Issue B. Null result on restricting omitted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "ASMC predicted rising body dissatisfaction but not binge eating or restraint."
- **Abstract says:** "ASMC significantly predicted increases in body dissatisfaction but did not predict changes in binge eating, cognitive restraint, or restricting."
- **Problem:** ASMC also failed to predict restricting directly; the link to restriction is only via the indirect path. Dropping "restricting" from the list of nulls lets a reader infer a direct effect that was not found.
- **Suggested fix:** "ASMC predicted rising body dissatisfaction but not binge eating, cognitive restraint or restricting directly."

---

### Study 6: People recovering from anorexia describe a phase of relentless hunger that clinical textbooks don't mention
**PMID:** 41983301 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

987 posts, r/AnorexiaRecovery, 25 July 2023–4 January 2024, 92 posts (9.3%), and all three themes are reported faithfully.

**Issue A. "Predictable, biologically plausible stage" goes beyond the data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A predictable, biologically plausible stage of recovery is going unexplained by clinicians"
- **Abstract says:** "Further research is needed to clarify its prevalence, underlying mechanisms, and clinical significance."
- **Problem:** The authors explicitly do not know how common extreme hunger is, why it occurs, or whether it is a normative phase. Describing it as a predictable stage with a known biological basis asserts exactly what the paper says is unresolved.
- **Suggested fix:** "An experience that recovering patients describe repeatedly has no established clinical account — its prevalence and mechanism are unknown — and the resulting fear appears to push some people back into restriction."

---

### Study 7: Ozempic has been absorbed into pro-eating-disorder Twitter as everyday, normalized talk
**PMID:** 42604953 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Netnography, "Ozempic" + "edtwt", August 2024–July 2025, 451 retrieved and 255 analysed, and every percentage (28.6, 19.2, 11.8, 11.4, 9.0, 3.5) matches the abstract. Author/institution correct.

**Issue A. Pitch reassigns a combined category to risk warnings alone** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The number to lead on is 3.5% — the share of posts containing any risk warning"
- **Abstract says:** "Information sharing and risk warnings accounted for 3.5% of posts."
- **Problem:** 3.5% is a combined category covering both information sharing *and* risk warnings; the risk-warning share alone is necessarily smaller and is not reported. The digest body states this correctly, but the pitch line does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "The number to lead on is 3.5% — the combined share of posts offering information or any risk warning"

---

### Study 8: Classmates can reliably name the school's "influencers" — and those teens are both kinder and more aggressive than their peers
**PMID:** 42552601 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=331, 7th and 8th graders, Midwestern school in a small community, peer-nomination measure, and the direction of the associations are all accurate. Author and institution correct.

**Issue A. "Reliably" overstates "moderate correspondence"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Classmates can reliably name the school's 'influencers'"
- **Abstract says:** "Peer-reported social media visibility showed moderate correspondence with various self-reports of social media use."
- **Problem:** Moderate correspondence with self-reported use is not "reliably." The digest body gets this right ("corresponded moderately"), so the headline is out of step with its own text.
- **Suggested fix:** "Classmates can broadly pick out the school's 'influencers'"

**Issue B. Causal verb and an aggression breakdown the abstract doesn't report** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and predicted higher levels of prosocial behavior, higher physical, verbal and relational aggression, and more self-reported substance use"
- **Abstract says:** "It was also associated with higher levels of prosocial and aggressive behavior and substance use."
- **Problem:** Two things. "Predicted" implies temporal ordering in a cross-sectional design. And while physical, verbal and relational aggression were each *measured*, the abstract reports the association only for aggression in aggregate — separate significance for each subtype is unverifiable from the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "and was associated with higher prosocial behaviour, higher aggression, and more self-reported substance use"

**Issue C. "Most-followed kid" misdescribes the measure** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the most-followed kid in year 8"
- **Abstract says:** "Social media visibility was assessed via peer nominations"
- **Problem:** No follower counts were collected; the construct is peer-perceived visibility, which is not the same thing and is the whole methodological point of the paper.
- **Suggested fix:** "the classmate everyone names as the most visible online"

---

### Study 9: A substantial minority of people press "like" specifically to hurt someone
**PMID:** 42424914 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The four-study structure, the five-year archival trend, schadenfreude as the dominant stated motive, the correlation in Study 3, and the Study 4 finding about those bothered by receiving such likes are all accurately summarised. Author and institution correct.

**Issue A. Headline merges two different findings** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "A substantial minority of people press 'like' specifically to hurt someone"
- **Abstract says:** "Results indicate a substantial minority of subjects engage in 'liking' negative outcomes of opponents, with most indicating schadenfreude as primary motivation" and, separately, "a significant number of subjects indicate they engage in the behavior to hurt the other party."
- **Problem:** The "substantial minority" figure describes people who do counter-valenced liking at all, whose main stated motive was schadenfreude (enjoying the pain), not intent to inflict it. The "to hurt the other party" group is an unquantified subset from a different study. The headline welds the size of one group onto the motive of another.
- **Suggested fix:** "A substantial minority of people press 'like' on a rival's bad news — and some say they do it to hurt"

---

### Study 10: Adding a social network to an eating-disorder app didn't help teens — and unguided self-help worked about as well as coaching
**PMID:** 41992076 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=148, three arms, recruitment via social media and an online screen, follow-up to 6 months, the null on global ED psychopathology, d = −0.93, and the faster binge-eating reduction in the GSH arm are all correct. The declared consultancies (Rissana, PredictView, Woebot, Kooth, Google Health) are properly carried into the Caveats.

**Issue A. Headline's second clause sits awkwardly with the abstract's conclusion** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and unguided self-help worked about as well as coaching"
- **Abstract says:** "with coaching possibly augmenting outcomes for some subgroups" and "the rate of reduction [in binge eating] was greatest in the GSH condition (p < 0.001)"
- **Problem:** True for the primary outcome, but the one significant differential effect favoured the coached arm. The headline states the equivalence without the qualifier the authors themselves attach.
- **Suggested fix:** "and unguided self-help matched coaching on the main outcome — though coaching led on binge eating"

**Issue B. "The simpler product" is ambiguous and points the wrong way** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this pilot finds no benefit, and hints the simpler product may be better for binge eating"
- **Abstract says:** "the rate of reduction was greatest in the GSH condition"
- **Problem:** The best-performing arm for binge eating was guided self-help — the arm *with* a human coach. A reader will most naturally read "the simpler product" as the plain unguided app, which was not the winner.
- **Suggested fix:** "this pilot finds no benefit from the social feature, and hints that the coached version without a social network did best on binge eating"

---

### Study 11: Four in five adolescents who self-harm or restrict say they sometimes do it to feel *worse*
**PMID:** 42010304 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=137, mean age 15.10, 75.18% female, online recruitment via social media from a larger longitudinal study, 81% endorsing at least one contra-hedonic function, and the NSSI/self-punishment findings are all accurately reported. Corresponding author at Yale is correct.

**Issue A. "Instead" turns an addition into a replacement** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The field has assumed these behaviors are pro-hedonic — done to reduce negative feeling. Instead, 81% endorsed at least one *contra*-hedonic function"
- **Abstract says:** "adolescents may not only engage in these behaviors to feel better, but also to make themselves feel worse"
- **Problem:** Pro-hedonic functions were also assessed and are not disconfirmed. The finding is that contra-hedonic motives coexist, not that they displace pro-hedonic ones — and the 81% figure is "at least one," not "primarily." The "Overturns prior research" label and the "targeting the wrong function" line in Why it matters both build on the exclusive reading.
- **Suggested fix:** "The field has treated these behaviours as pro-hedonic — done to reduce negative feeling. In addition to that, 81% endorsed at least one *contra*-hedonic function..." and relabel novelty as "Challenges a prevailing assumption."

---

### Study 12: Identifying with an online group makes you more likely to start measuring yourself against others
**PMID:** 42546360 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Country-by-country Ns (1541/1561/1529/1112/1533), age range 18–75, within- and between-person effects, and partial mediation by self-verification are all accurate.

**Issue A. Causal headline for observational panel data** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Identifying with an online group makes you more likely to start measuring yourself against others"
- **Abstract says:** "Online social identification might make us more susceptible to ability comparisons" (title) and "group identification was associated with positive within-person and between-person changes in ability comparison orientation"
- **Problem:** "Makes you" is a causal claim from correlational panel data; the authors hedge with "might" in their own title. The digest's own Caveats say the design "cannot establish causation," so the headline contradicts the caveat. "Start measuring yourself" also implies onset, whereas the outcome is a continuous comparison-orientation score.
- **Suggested fix:** "Identifying with an online group goes with a stronger pull to measure yourself against others"

---

### Study 13: The strongest predictor of compulsive short-video use isn't the pull of the videos — it's overestimating your own self-control
**PMID:** 42608804 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=842, PLS-SEM, overestimation of self-control as the strongest driver exceeding the total effect of flow, and flow's indirect route via that overestimation are all reported accurately. Author and institution correct.

**Issue A. Flow's dimensions are mislabelled** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "treating 'flow' not as the classic optimal experience but as a passive state with maladaptive components (affective reliance, loss of self-reflection, telepresence)"
- **Abstract says:** "flow is reconceptualized as a passive psychological state comprising both immersive and maladaptive dimensions (i.e., concentration, enjoyment, telepresence, heightened arousal, affective reliance, and loss of self-reflection)" and "concentration, telepresence, and affective reliance significantly intensifying compulsive use and/or overestimation of self-control"
- **Problem:** Telepresence is listed among the six dimensions without being designated maladaptive, and loss of self-reflection — which the digest lists as a maladaptive component — was *not* among the dimensions that significantly intensified compulsive use. Concentration, which was significant, is omitted.
- **Suggested fix:** "treating 'flow' as a passive state with six dimensions, both immersive and maladaptive; concentration, telepresence and affective reliance were the ones that significantly intensified compulsive use or self-control overconfidence"

---

### Study 14: Short-form video use predicts disordered eating four months later — in working nurses, not teenagers
**PMID:** 41968956 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=400 at baseline, 270 at four-month follow-up (32.5% attrition), single Wuhan hospital, female registered nurses, indirect effect via body dissatisfaction, moderation by perceived media pressure and thin-ideal internalisation — all accurate. Authors and institution correct.

**Issue A. "Increased body dissatisfaction" implies change that was not measured** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Baseline short-form video use predicted disordered eating at follow-up indirectly, through increased body dissatisfaction."
- **Abstract says:** "Measures assessed short-form video use and sociocultural attitudes at T1 and body dissatisfaction and disordered eating at T2."
- **Problem:** Body dissatisfaction was only measured at follow-up, so there is no baseline against which an increase could be observed, and mediator and outcome were assessed simultaneously. "Increased" implies a within-person change the two-wave design cannot show. Worth adding to Caveats, which currently only says "two waves."
- **Suggested fix:** "Baseline short-form video use predicted disordered eating at follow-up indirectly, via body dissatisfaction measured at the same follow-up point."

*Note: "shift-working" (Why it matters) and "after a night shift" (pitch) are plausible but unverifiable from the abstract, which reports no shift-work data.*

---

### Study 15: One capacity — the ability to get started — sits underneath anxiety, depression, drinking and compulsive social media use
**PMID:** 42285011 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=1,997 community adults, the predictor set, Bayesian model averaging, initiatory self-control across all four outcomes, emotional abuse and anxious attachment for anxiety/depression/PSMU, and psychological flexibility for internalizing but not behavioural outcomes are all accurate. ## Editor's note on patterns

Three recurring problems are worth fixing systematically rather than entry by entry:

**Headlines drifting past their own body text.** Studies 8, 12 and 23 all contain accurate body copy and accurate caveats, then a headline that contradicts them. Study 23 is the sharpest case: the abstract says the reductions "cannot be firmly attributed to the interventions," the digest's caveat repeats that verbatim in substance, and the headline says the exercise "reduced trauma symptoms." Headlines are the part of a digest that survives into a pitch email, so they need the same causal discipline as the body.

**Composite or combined statistics split apart.** Studies 7 and 9 both take a figure describing one thing and attach it to a narrower, more striking thing — 3.5% for "information sharing and risk warnings" becomes 3.5% for risk warnings; "a substantial minority" who like rival misfortune becomes "a substantial minority" who do it to hurt. Both would be embarrassing to have quoted back by a source.

**NS fit scores.** Only Study 1 needs a downward adjustment on my read (7→6). The remaining 7s — Studies 2, 3 and 4 — are defensible: Study 2 has N=6,153 across three waves, Study 3 has five studies including two experiments, Study 4 has 858 participants under intensive momentary sampling. Their weaknesses are self-report rather than sample size, and the digest names that weakness in each fit line. The scores of 6 and below are all appropriately calibrated, and Studies 16, 17, 19 and 22 in particular are scored honestly against thin or preliminary evidence.

**Items needing full-text or external verification before pitching:** the "samples are largely Chinese" caveat on Study 3; the shift-work framing on Study 14; the cumulative-neurological-effects angle on Study 21; and the field-wide claim in Study 2's wider angle that RI-CLPM has been "erasing 'bidirectional' screen findings across the field."
